title: Romans in 8 Weeks
subtitle: The gospel, start to finish
tagline: Not ashamed of the gospel, from the first verse to the last.
about: Over eight weeks you will read all sixteen chapters of Paul's letter to the Romans, a short passage each weekday. You will follow Paul's argument from humanity's need, to God's righteousness given through faith in Christ, to new life in the Spirit, to God's faithfulness to Israel, and finally to what love looks like in a real church. You will come away understanding why Romans has shaped Christian faith for nearly two thousand years.

days.title: Not Ashamed of the Gospel
days.focus: Paul introduces himself and his message, then states the theme of the whole letter in verses 16–17. Notice what he says the gospel is about (God's Son, descended from David, declared Son of God by the resurrection) and what it does.
days.context: Paul wrote around AD 57, most likely from Corinth, to a church he had never visited. He hoped to stop in Rome on his way to preach in Spain (15:24).

word.why: Paul uses this word in his first verse and in his theme statement (v. 16). In the wider world it could announce good news such as a victory or a new ruler; Paul's good news concerns God's Son and is 'the power of God unto salvation.'

questions.q: What two things does Paul say about God's Son in verses 3–4?
What does Paul mean when he calls the gospel 'the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth'?
When, if ever, have you felt ashamed of the gospel, and what was behind that feeling?

checkIn.q: What does Paul say he is not ashamed of?
Paul calls himself a servant of whom?

days.title: Exchanging the Truth
days.focus: Paul begins his case that all people need rescue. Notice the pattern of exchange (people 'changed' God's glory and truth for something less) and the repeated phrase 'God gave them up.'
days.context: Jewish writers of the time often criticized Gentile idolatry in similar terms, so many of Paul's first listeners would have nodded along. That sets up the surprise at the start of chapter 2.

word.why: 'The wrath of God is revealed from heaven' (v. 18). This is not a fit of temper but God's settled opposition to evil, shown here partly by handing people over to the results of their own choices (vv. 24, 26, 28).

questions.q: What does Paul say people can know about God from creation (v. 20)?
What does it mean that people 'changed the truth of God into a lie' and worshipped the creature rather than the Creator (v. 25)?
Which good gifts are you most tempted to treat as if they were God?

checkIn.q: What phrase does Paul repeat to describe God's response?
What does Paul say is clearly seen from the creation of the world?

days.title: No Room to Judge
days.focus: Paul turns to anyone who has been nodding along at chapter 1. Notice the 'Therefore' in verse 1 and the principle that God judges without favoritism, according to truth and to what people have done.
days.context: Paul speaks to an imaginary conversation partner ('O man'), a teaching style of the day in which a writer answers the objections of a pretend listener.

word.why: 'The goodness of God leadeth thee to repentance' (v. 4). God's patience is not approval; his kindness is meant to turn people around, not give them a reason to relax.

questions.q: What does Paul say God's goodness is meant to lead people to (v. 4)?
How do verses 14–15 describe Gentiles who do not have the written law?
When have you mistaken God's patience for his approval?

checkIn.q: According to verse 11, what is there none of with God?
Paul says the person who judges others does what?

days.title: Circumcision of the Heart
days.focus: Paul now addresses the Jewish teacher who relies on having the law. Notice the list of real privileges, the pointed questions that follow, and Paul's closing description of a true Jew.
days.context: Circumcision was the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and a central mark of Jewish identity, setting Jews apart from the surrounding nations.

word.why: Paul does not call circumcision worthless (v. 25), but he insists the real thing is 'that of the heart, in the spirit' (v. 29), an idea already found in Moses and the prophets.

questions.q: What questions does Paul put to the one who teaches others (vv. 21–23)?
What does Paul mean by circumcision 'of the heart'?
Which outward religious marks do you lean on to feel secure with God?

checkIn.q: According to verse 24, what happens among the Gentiles because of those who break the law?
options: The name of God is blasphemed

checkIn.q: Where does Paul say true circumcision is?
options: Of the heart, in the spirit

days.title: None Righteous, No, Not One
days.focus: Paul answers objections and then strings together Old Testament quotations showing that all are 'under sin.' Notice how the quotations move through the body: throat, tongue, lips, mouth, feet, eyes.
days.context: Verses 10–18 are a chain of Old Testament texts, mainly from the Psalms and Isaiah. Jewish teachers often linked passages together like this to make a point.

word.why: 'There is none righteous, no, not one' (v. 10). The word describes someone who is in the right before God; Paul's case is that no one qualifies on their own, which prepares for God's own righteousness in verse 21.

questions.q: What advantage does Paul say the Jews have (v. 2)?
If the law cannot make anyone righteous, what does verse 20 say it does?
How do you respond inwardly when Paul says 'all the world' is guilty before God?

checkIn.q: What was committed to the Jews, according to verse 2?
What comes by the law, according to verse 20?

days.title: But Now: Righteousness Revealed
days.focus: 'But now' marks the turning point of the letter. Notice the words Paul piles up (righteousness, faith, grace, redemption, propitiation) and how often he stresses 'all.'
days.context: 'Redemption' was a word for buying a slave's freedom. 'Propitiation' points to the mercy seat, the lid of the ark of the covenant, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement.

word.meaning: propitiation, mercy seat, place of atonement
word.why: This is the word used for the mercy seat in the Greek Old Testament and in Hebrews 9:5. Paul says God 'set forth' Christ as this place of atonement (v. 25), where sin is dealt with and God's justice and mercy meet.

questions.q: According to verse 23, who has sinned?
How can God be both 'just' and 'the justifier of him which believeth in Jesus' (v. 26)?
What does it mean to you that you are justified 'freely by his grace'?

checkIn.q: What does Paul say is excluded (v. 27)?
Does faith make the law void, according to verse 31?
options: God forbid: we establish the law

days.title: Abraham Believed God
days.focus: Paul uses Abraham as his test case. Notice the timing argument: Abraham was counted righteous before he was circumcised, which makes him the father of all who believe.
days.context: Abraham was the founding father of the Jewish people, and many Jewish teachers held him up as a model of faithful obedience. Paul quotes Genesis 15:6 and Psalm 32.

word.meaning: to count, to reckon, to credit
word.why: This accounting word appears again and again in chapter 4. 'Abraham believed God, and it was counted unto him for righteousness' (v. 3); righteousness is credited as a gift, not paid as wages (v. 4).

questions.q: Whom does Paul quote besides Abraham in verses 6–8, and what does he say?
Why does it matter whether Abraham was counted righteous before or after his circumcision?
Do you tend to relate to God more like an employer paying wages or like a giver of gifts?

checkIn.q: Whom does Paul quote alongside Abraham?
When was faith counted to Abraham for righteousness?

days.title: Hope Against Hope
days.focus: Paul looks at God's promise to Abraham and how Abraham trusted it against impossible odds. Notice that Abraham faced the facts (his body 'now dead') and still believed.
days.context: Abraham was about a hundred years old and Sarah about ninety when God promised them a son (Genesis 17:17).

word.why: The promise came 'not ... through the law, but through the righteousness of faith' (v. 13). Because it rests on God's promise rather than human performance, it is 'sure to all the seed' (v. 16), Jew and Gentile alike.

questions.q: What does Paul say about who God is in verse 17?
Why does the kind of God described in verse 17 make Abraham's faith reasonable rather than blind?
Where are you being asked to hope 'against hope' right now?

checkIn.q: About how old was Abraham?
How did Abraham respond to God's promise?
options: He was strong in faith, giving glory to God

days.title: Peace with God
days.focus: Paul describes what justification brings: peace, access, hope, and God's love poured into our hearts. Notice the timing phrases: 'without strength,' 'yet sinners,' 'enemies.'
days.context: This passage marks a shift from how people are justified to what life looks like afterward. Paul's 'we' now includes himself and his readers as people already reconciled.

word.why: 'When we were enemies, we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son' (v. 10). Reconciliation is relational: hostility turned to friendship, with God taking the first step.

questions.q: What chain does Paul describe beginning with tribulation (vv. 3–4)?
How does verse 8 show God's love differently than if Christ had died for good people?
Which of the phrases 'without strength,' 'yet sinners,' or 'enemies' speaks most to you, and why?

checkIn.q: According to verse 3, what does tribulation work?
When did Christ die for us?

days.title: Adam and Christ
days.focus: Paul compares two representatives of humanity: Adam brought sin and death; Christ brings grace and life. Notice the 'much more' statements that show the two are not evenly matched.
days.context: Paul treats Adam as the head of humanity whose choice affected everyone after him. Christians have explained the link between Adam's sin and ours in different ways, but agree that Paul's main point is the greater power of Christ's grace.

word.why: 'Where sin abounded, grace did much more abound' (v. 20). Grace is God's undeserved favor, and in verse 21 Paul pictures it reigning like a king where sin and death once ruled.

questions.q: Find the 'much more' statements in this passage. What two things is Paul comparing each time?
What does it mean that grace 'reigns' (v. 21)?
Where are you most aware of sin's reach, and where have you seen grace reach further?

checkIn.q: Through whom does the gift of righteousness come?
Where sin abounded, what did much more abound?

days.title: Dead to Sin, Alive to God
days.focus: Paul answers an objection: if grace abounds where sin abounds, why not keep sinning? Notice the picture of dying, being buried, and rising with Christ, and the commands to 'reckon' and to 'yield.'
days.context: Most early believers were baptized soon after coming to faith, so Paul could assume his readers remembered their own baptism.

word.why: 'So many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death' (v. 3); the word means to dip or immerse, and Paul uses it to picture union with Christ in his death and resurrection. Christians differ on the mode and meaning of baptism, but all read this passage as describing that union.

questions.q: What question does Paul ask in verse 1, and how does he answer it?
What does it mean to 'reckon' yourself dead to sin but alive to God (v. 11)?
Which part of your life do you find hardest to 'yield' to God?

checkIn.q: Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?
Sin shall not have dominion over you, for you are not under the law but under what?

days.title: Wages and Gift
days.focus: Paul uses the picture of slavery to say that everyone serves someone. Notice where each kind of service leads, and the final contrast between wages and a gift.
days.context: Slavery was everywhere in the Roman world, and many in the Roman church were slaves or freed slaves. Paul says he speaks 'after the manner of men' (v. 19), using an image his readers knew well.

word.why: The word described a soldier's ration money or pay. Sin pays wages, and those wages are death; eternal life is not wages at all but 'the gift of God' (v. 23).

questions.q: What does Paul say came from the things his readers are now ashamed of (v. 21)?
Why does Paul call eternal life a 'gift' rather than wages?
Besides God, what masters compete for your obedience?

checkIn.q: What are the wages of sin?
What is the gift of God?
options: Eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord

days.title: Released from the Law
days.focus: Paul uses marriage to explain how believers now relate to the law: a death ends the obligation. Notice the purpose of this release: to belong to another, Christ, and 'bring forth fruit unto God.'
days.context: Paul says he is speaking 'to them that know the law' (v. 1), probably Jewish believers and Gentiles who had spent time in the synagogue.

word.meaning: to release, to make inactive, to bring to an end
word.why: A widow is 'loosed from the law of her husband' (v. 2), and believers are 'delivered from the law' (v. 6). The word means something is no longer in force over a person; it does not mean the law was bad.

questions.q: When, according to verses 2–3, is a wife free from the law of her husband?
What does Paul mean by serving 'in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter' (v. 6)?
Do you relate to God more out of obligation or out of belonging?

checkIn.q: What relationship does Paul use as his example?
Believers are to be married to whom?
options: Him who is raised from the dead

days.title: Is the Law Sin?
days.focus: Paul insists the law is holy, yet sin used the commandment to bring death. Notice his example, 'Thou shalt not covet,' and the way sin is described almost like an enemy lying in wait.
days.context: Paul speaks in the first person here. Interpreters differ on whether 'I' describes Paul's own experience, Adam's, Israel's at Sinai, or humanity in general.

word.why: 'I had not known lust, except the law had said, Thou shalt not covet' (v. 7). The commandment named the desire, and sin seized the opportunity to stir up 'all manner of concupiscence' (v. 8), an old word for strong desire.

questions.q: How does Paul describe the law and the commandment in verse 12?
If the law is good, how did it become an occasion for death?
Have you noticed that being told 'don't' can make something more tempting? What does that reveal?

checkIn.q: Which commandment does Paul use as his example?
How does Paul describe the commandment?

days.title: O Wretched Man
days.focus: Paul describes a painful inner conflict: wanting the good but not doing it. Notice the cry of verse 24 and the answer that follows immediately in verse 25.
days.context: Christians have long disagreed about whether Paul is describing life as a believer, his life before Christ, or someone under the law without the Spirit. Each view has thoughtful defenders.

word.why: 'O wretched man that I am!' (v. 24) uses a word for someone worn down by hardship. Paul's cry is followed at once by thanksgiving, which leads straight into chapter 8.

questions.q: What question does Paul ask in verse 24, and how does he answer it in verse 25?
What does Paul mean by 'sin that dwelleth in me' (vv. 17, 20)?
Where do you most feel the gap between what you want to do and what you actually do?

checkIn.q: What does Paul say he finds himself doing?
options: The good that he wants to do
The evil that he does not want to do

checkIn.q: Whom does Paul thank for deliverance?
options: God through Jesus Christ our Lord

days.title: No Condemnation
days.focus: Paul announces 'no condemnation' and explains how: God sent his Son, and the Spirit now gives life. Notice the contrast between the flesh and the Spirit, and the promise about resurrection at the end.
days.context: In Paul's letters, 'flesh' often means human nature living apart from God, not simply the physical body.

word.why: This is a legal word for the verdict and the sentence that follows. 'There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus' (v. 1), because God 'condemned sin in the flesh' through his Son (v. 3).

questions.q: What did God do that the law could not do (v. 3)?
What is the difference between being 'in the flesh' and being 'in the Spirit'?
Where are you still living as though you were under condemnation?

checkIn.q: To whom is there no condemnation?
options: To them which are in Christ Jesus
To those who keep the law

checkIn.q: What will the Spirit of him that raised up Jesus do (v. 11)?

days.title: Abba, Father
days.focus: Paul moves from the language of debt to the language of family. Notice what those led by the Spirit are called, what they cry out, and how being heirs is tied to sharing Christ's sufferings.
days.context: In Roman law, an adopted son received full legal standing as his new father's child and heir. 'Abba' is the Aramaic word for father that Jesus used in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36).

word.why: 'Ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father' (v. 15). Believers are not tolerated guests in God's house but children with a full place in the family.

questions.q: What does the Spirit bear witness to (v. 16)?
How does adoption change the way a person relates to God?
Do you approach God more like a nervous servant or like a beloved child?

checkIn.q: What does the Spirit of adoption lead us to cry?
If children, then what?
options: Heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ

days.title: Groaning and Hope
days.focus: Paul sets present suffering beside future glory. Notice the three groanings: creation groans, believers groan, and the Spirit groans on our behalf.
days.context: Paul pictures the whole created world as waiting, which recalls the curse on the ground in Genesis 3 and the prophets' hope of a renewed creation.

word.why: 'The Spirit itself maketh intercession for us with groanings which cannot be uttered' (v. 26). When believers do not know what to pray, God's own Spirit prays within their weakness.

questions.q: Who or what groans in this passage?
What is creation waiting for (vv. 19–21)?
What are you groaning over right now, and how does verse 26 speak to it?

checkIn.q: How does Paul compare present sufferings with the glory to come?
options: They are not worthy to be compared

checkIn.q: What does the Spirit do when we know not what to pray for?

days.title: All Things for Good
days.focus: Paul gives a famous promise followed by an unbroken chain: foreknew, predestinated, called, justified, glorified. Notice the purpose stated in the middle: to be conformed to the image of God's Son.
days.context: Christians have long understood 'foreknow' and 'predestinate' in different ways, some stressing God's sovereign choice and others his foreknowledge of faith. All read these verses as a comfort that God finishes what he begins.

word.why: God's purpose is that his people be 'conformed to the image of his Son' (v. 29). The 'good' of verse 28 is defined here: becoming like Christ, the firstborn among many brethren.

questions.q: List the five links in the chain in verses 29–30.
How does verse 29 help define the 'good' promised in verse 28?
What difficult situation in your life is hardest to imagine God working for good?

checkIn.q: All things work together for good to whom?
options: To them that love God, who are the called

checkIn.q: To whose image are believers to be conformed?

days.title: More Than Conquerors
days.focus: Paul ends chapter 8 with questions no one can answer against God's people. Notice the list of things that cannot separate believers from God's love.
days.context: In verse 36 Paul quotes Psalm 44:22, a lament in which God's people suffer even though they have been faithful.

word.meaning: to be more than a conqueror, to win overwhelmingly
word.why: 'Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us' (v. 37). The victory comes not by escaping trouble but in the middle of it, and not by our strength but 'through him.'

questions.q: What questions does Paul ask in verses 31–35?
How does verse 32 argue from the greater gift to the lesser?
Which item in verses 38–39 do you most fear could separate you from God's love?

checkIn.q: If God be for us, who can be what?
Can anything in all creation separate us from the love of God in Christ?

days.title: Has God's Word Failed?
days.focus: Paul expresses deep grief for his fellow Israelites and asks whether God's promise has failed. Notice his examples from Genesis: Isaac rather than Ishmael, Jacob rather than Esau.
days.context: Romans 9–11 wrestles with why many of Paul's fellow Jews had not believed in Jesus as the Messiah. Christians read these chapters in different ways, some seeing God's choice of individuals for salvation and others his choice of people and nations for roles in his plan.

word.why: 'That the purpose of God according to election might stand' (v. 11): God's promise has always moved forward by his choice, not by birth or deeds. How this applies to individual salvation is one of the great questions on which thoughtful Christians differ.

questions.q: What privileges of Israel does Paul list in verses 4–5?
What does Paul mean by 'they are not all Israel, which are of Israel' (v. 6)?
Paul's grief for his people is deep (vv. 2–3). For whom do you feel that kind of grief?

checkIn.q: How does Paul describe his feelings for his kinsmen?
options: Great heaviness and continual sorrow in his heart

checkIn.q: Through whom does Paul say Abraham's seed would be called?

days.title: Mercy and the Potter
days.focus: Paul raises the objection 'Is there unrighteousness with God?' Notice his examples (Moses and Pharaoh), the potter and the clay, and the prophets' words about Gentiles and a remnant.
days.context: The potter-and-clay picture comes from the prophets (Isaiah 29:16; Jeremiah 18). Christians read this passage in different ways, as God's sovereign choice of individuals or as his freedom to shape his plan and show mercy widely, and humility suits every reading.

word.meaning: to have mercy, to show compassion
word.why: 'I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy' (v. 15) quotes Exodus 33:19. Mercy is never owed; it flows from God's freedom, and Paul's argument ends with mercy reaching Gentiles who 'were not my people' (v. 25).

questions.q: Which Old Testament figures and prophets does Paul cite in this passage?
How does the potter image respond to the objection 'Why doth he yet find fault?' (v. 19)?
How do you respond when God's ways are beyond your understanding?

checkIn.q: To whom did God say 'I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy'?
Which prophet does Paul quote about a remnant being saved?

days.title: Christ, the End of the Law
days.focus: Paul explains a surprise: Gentiles found righteousness by faith, while Israel pursued the law and stumbled. Notice the 'stumblingstone' and Paul's heartfelt prayer for Israel.
days.context: Paul blends Isaiah 8:14 and 28:16 for the image of a stone that some trip over and others trust in; Peter uses the same texts (1 Peter 2:6-8).

word.why: 'Christ is the end of the law for righteousness' (10:4) uses a word that can mean an ending or a goal, like the finish line of a race. Many readers think Paul means something of both, that the law pointed to Christ and reaches its purpose in him, though Christians weigh these senses differently.

questions.q: What does Paul pray for Israel (10:1)?
What does Paul mean by 'a zeal of God, but not according to knowledge' (10:2)?
Where might you be zealous for God in a way that misses what he is actually doing?

checkIn.q: What did the Gentiles attain?
What did Israel stumble at?

days.title: Confess and Believe
days.focus: Paul contrasts two ways of seeking righteousness and shows how near the word of faith is. Notice the pairing of mouth and heart, and the wide promise of verse 13.
days.context: Paul draws on Deuteronomy 30:12-14, where Moses told Israel that God's word was not far off but near. 'Jesus is Lord' was one of the earliest Christian confessions.

word.meaning: to confess, to acknowledge, to agree
word.why: 'If thou shalt confess with thy mouth the Lord Jesus' (v. 9). The word literally means to say the same thing, so to confess is to agree openly with God about who Jesus is.

questions.q: Where does Paul say the word of faith is (v. 8)?
Why might Paul pair confessing with the mouth and believing in the heart?
What makes it easy or hard for you to say aloud that Jesus is Lord?

checkIn.q: Whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be what?
What does Paul say about Jew and Greek in verse 12?
options: There is no difference: the same Lord over all

days.title: How Shall They Hear?
days.focus: Paul traces how faith comes: sending, preaching, hearing, believing, calling. Notice the 'beautiful feet' and the closing image of God holding out his hands all day long.
days.context: Paul quotes Isaiah, Moses, and the Psalms to show that Israel's mixed response to the message had been foreseen in their own scriptures.

word.why: 'Faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God' (v. 17). The same word is translated 'report' in verse 16 ('who hath believed our report?'), so it means both the act of hearing and the message heard.

questions.q: List the chain of questions in verses 14–15.
What does God's outstretched hand 'all day long' (v. 21) say about him?
Who first brought the good news to you, and what did it cost them?

checkIn.q: Whose feet does Paul call beautiful?
options: Them that preach the gospel of peace

checkIn.q: Faith comes by what?

days.title: A Remnant by Grace
days.focus: Paul asks, 'Hath God cast away his people?' and answers with his own story and Elijah's. Notice the phrase 'a remnant according to the election of grace.'
days.context: Elijah once believed he was the only faithful Israelite left, but God told him seven thousand had not bowed to Baal (1 Kings 19).

word.why: 'There is a remnant according to the election of grace' (v. 5). Throughout Israel's history God preserved a faithful remnant, and Paul and other Jewish believers in Jesus are evidence that God has not abandoned his people.

questions.q: What evidence from his own life does Paul give that God has not cast away his people?
How does Elijah's story support Paul's argument?
Have you ever felt, like Elijah, that you were alone in faithfulness? What does God's answer to him say to you?

checkIn.q: Which tribe does Paul say he is from?
How many men had God reserved who had not bowed to Baal?

days.title: The Olive Tree
days.focus: Paul pictures God's people as an olive tree: some natural branches broken off, wild branches grafted in. Notice the warnings to Gentile believers against boasting, and the hope that natural branches can be grafted in again.
days.context: Olive trees were common across the Mediterranean, and growers grafted branches to improve them. Paul admits that grafting a wild branch into a cultivated tree is 'contrary to nature' (v. 24).

word.why: Paul uses this word repeatedly in verses 17–24. A grafted branch draws life from a root it did not grow from; Gentile believers share in Israel's story rather than replacing it.

questions.q: What does Paul warn the grafted-in branches not to do (v. 18)?
What does it mean that 'thou bearest not the root, but the root thee' (v. 18)?
Where might spiritual pride creep into how you view other believers?

checkIn.q: What kind of tree does Paul use as his picture?
Can the natural branches be grafted in again?
options: Yes, if they abide not still in unbelief

days.title: O the Depth!
days.focus: Paul reveals a 'mystery' about Israel's future and then breaks into praise. Notice that the long argument of chapters 9–11 ends not in a formula but in worship.
days.context: 'All Israel shall be saved' (v. 26) has been read in several ways: as a future turning of the Jewish people to Christ, as the full number of God's people from Jews and Gentiles, or as the faithful remnant through history. Thoughtful Christians hold each of these views.

word.meaning: mystery, something once hidden now revealed
word.why: In Paul's letters a mystery is not a puzzle to solve but something God has now made known (v. 25). Here it concerns Israel's partial hardening 'until the fulness of the Gentiles be come in.'

questions.q: What does Paul say about the gifts and calling of God (v. 29)?
Why do you think Paul ends this long argument with praise (vv. 33–36)?
Which of God's ways do you find most 'past finding out,' and what would it mean to praise him there?

checkIn.q: What does Paul say about God's gifts and calling?
How does Paul end chapter 11?
options: With praise: to whom be glory for ever

days.title: A Living Sacrifice
days.focus: The 'therefore' of 12:1 turns from God's mercies to how believers live. Notice the call to present bodies, the renewed mind, and the different gifts within one body.
days.context: Paul's readers knew sacrifices as animals killed on altars; he calls instead for a 'living sacrifice.' The phrase 'reasonable service' can also be translated 'spiritual worship.'

word.why: 'Be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind' (v. 2). The same word describes Jesus' transfiguration (Matthew 17:2) and points to a deep change from the inside rather than a shape pressed on from outside.

questions.q: What gifts does Paul list in verses 6–8?
What is the difference between being 'conformed to this world' and being 'transformed'?
Which gift in this list might God have given you, and how are you using it?

checkIn.q: What does Paul urge believers to present to God?
How should a person think of himself, according to verse 3?

days.title: Love Without Pretending
days.focus: A rapid series of short commands describes genuine love. Notice how the passage moves from love inside the church to love toward outsiders and even enemies.
days.context: 'Coals of fire on his head' (v. 20) quotes Proverbs 25:21-22. Many interpreters take it as a picture of an enemy brought to shame and remorse by kindness, though the exact image is debated.

word.why: 'Let love be without dissimulation' (v. 9). The word means literally 'un-hypocritical,' without an actor's mask, and everything that follows describes what unmasked love actually does.

questions.q: What does Paul say to do if an enemy is hungry or thirsty?
Why does Paul tell believers to leave vengeance to God (v. 19)?
Which of these commands do you find hardest to put into practice?

checkIn.q: How should evil be overcome?
Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with whom?

days.title: Governing Authorities
days.focus: Paul tells believers to be subject to governing authorities and to pay taxes and give honor. Notice the reasons he gives: authority is ordained by God and exists to restrain evil.
days.context: Paul wrote early in Nero's reign, a relatively stable period. Christians have long discussed the limits of this teaching, especially when rulers command what God forbids (compare Acts 5:29).

word.why: 'Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers' (v. 1). The word means rightful authority, and Paul grounds it in God ('there is no power but of God'), which both honors human rulers and places them under God.

questions.q: What does Paul tell believers to render to all (v. 7)?
What does Paul say rulers are for in verses 3–4?
How does your attitude toward leaders you disagree with compare with this passage?

checkIn.q: Where does Paul say all authority comes from?
Which of these does Paul tell believers to pay?

days.title: Put On Christ
days.focus: Paul sums up the law in love, then urges believers to wake up because the day is near. Notice the clothing language: cast off the works of darkness, put on the armour of light, put on the Lord Jesus Christ.
days.context: Augustine of Hippo wrote in his Confessions that reading verses 13–14 was the turning point of his conversion in AD 386.

word.meaning: to put on, to clothe oneself
word.why: 'Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ' (v. 14). Believers put on Christ the way they would put on clothing, a picture of taking on his character and identity day by day.

questions.q: Which commandments does Paul say are summed up in 'Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself'?
Why does knowing that 'the night is far spent' change how believers live now?
What would 'make not provision for the flesh' (v. 14) look like in your own week?

checkIn.q: What does Paul call the fulfilling of the law?
Whom does Paul tell believers to put on?

days.title: Welcome the Weak
days.focus: Paul addresses disputes over food and special days. Notice the commands to receive one another and not to judge or despise, and the reason: every believer belongs to the Lord.
days.context: Some believers, likely including many Jewish Christians, kept food laws or avoided meat, while others felt free to eat anything. Paul calls these groups the 'weak' and the 'strong' in faith.

word.meaning: to receive, to welcome, to take in
word.why: 'Him that is weak in the faith receive ye' (v. 1), for God 'hath received him' (v. 3). The word means to take someone in as a companion, and Paul returns to it in 15:7.

questions.q: What two disagreements does Paul mention in verses 2 and 5?
What does Paul mean by 'whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's' (v. 8)?
On which disputable matters are you most tempted to judge or look down on other believers?

checkIn.q: According to verse 2, what does the weak believer eat?
Before whose judgment seat will we all stand?

days.title: No Stumbling Block
days.focus: Paul moves from judging others to the danger of tripping them up. Notice his summary of the kingdom of God in verse 17.
days.context: Paul himself was persuaded that 'there is nothing unclean of itself' (v. 14), yet he puts love for others above his own freedom.

word.why: 'That no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother's way' (v. 13). The word first referred to the trigger of a trap; freedom used carelessly can become a trap for another believer.

questions.q: How does Paul describe the kingdom of God in verse 17?
What does Paul mean by 'whatsoever is not of faith is sin' (v. 23)?
Is there a freedom you enjoy that might be hard on someone else's faith?

checkIn.q: The kingdom of God is not meat and drink, but what?
options: Righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost

checkIn.q: What does Paul urge believers to follow after?
options: The things which make for peace

days.title: The God of Hope
days.focus: Paul points to Christ as the example of bearing with others, then shows from scripture that God always intended Jews and Gentiles to praise him together. Notice the blessing that closes the section.
days.context: In verses 9–12 Paul quotes the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms, and every quotation mentions the Gentiles.

word.why: The scriptures were written so 'that we ... might have hope' (v. 4), and Paul closes with a prayer to 'the God of hope' (v. 13). Hope here is not wishful thinking but confident expectation grounded in God's promises.

questions.q: Why does Paul say the scriptures were 'written aforetime' (v. 4)?
How does Christ's example in verses 3 and 7 shape how believers treat one another?
Who is the hardest person for you to 'receive' as Christ received you?

checkIn.q: Who ought to bear the infirmities of the weak?
What does Paul call God in verse 13?

days.title: A Priest of the Gospel
days.focus: Paul explains why he wrote so boldly and describes his ministry to the Gentiles. Notice his worship language, and his ambition to preach where Christ has not yet been named.
days.context: Illyricum (v. 19) lay along the eastern coast of the Adriatic Sea, in the region of the modern Balkans. Paul had preached in a great arc from Jerusalem to there.

word.why: Paul describes himself as 'ministering the gospel of God, that the offering up of the Gentiles might be acceptable' (v. 16). This word appears only here in the New Testament; Paul pictures his preaching as priestly service, with the Gentile believers themselves as the offering.

questions.q: From where to where does Paul say he has fully preached the gospel (v. 19)?
What does it mean to picture the Gentile believers as an 'offering'?
How might your ordinary work look different if you saw it as an offering to God?

checkIn.q: Where did Paul strive to preach the gospel?
To whom does Paul say he is the minister of Jesus Christ?

days.title: Plans for Spain
days.focus: Paul shares his travel plans: Jerusalem with a gift, then Rome, then Spain. Notice his earnest request for prayer and the dangers he expects.
days.context: Paul had been collecting money from Gentile churches for poor believers in Jerusalem (see 1 Corinthians 16 and 2 Corinthians 8–9). Acts records that he was arrested in Jerusalem and reached Rome as a prisoner (Acts 21–28).

word.why: The KJV translates it 'contribution' (v. 26). The gift was more than money; Gentile churches sharing with Jewish believers expressed their partnership in one family.

questions.q: What does Paul ask the Romans to pray for in verses 30–32?
Why does Paul say the Gentiles owe something to the believers in Jerusalem (v. 27)?
When you ask others to pray for you, how specific and honest are you?

checkIn.q: Where did Paul plan to go after visiting Rome?
What was Paul bringing to Jerusalem?
options: A contribution for the poor saints

days.title: Phoebe, Prisca, and Aquila
days.focus: Paul commends Phoebe and begins greeting people by name. Notice the variety (men and women, Jews and Gentiles) and the words of honor Paul uses for them.
days.context: Phoebe likely carried the letter to Rome; Cenchrea was the eastern port of Corinth. Priscilla and Aquila were tentmakers who had worked alongside Paul (Acts 18).

word.why: Paul calls Phoebe 'a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea' (v. 1). The word can mean a servant in general or the church office of deacon; Christians differ on which Paul meant here, but all agree he commends her highly.

questions.q: What does Paul say Priscilla and Aquila risked for him (v. 4)?
What does this list of names suggest about the church in Rome?
Who has gone out of their way for you in the faith, and have you ever told them?

checkIn.q: Whom does Paul commend at the start of chapter 16?
Where did a church meet, according to verse 5?
options: In the house of Priscilla and Aquila

days.title: Greet One Another
days.focus: Paul continues greeting people by name, often with a short word of description. Notice the warmth of his language: 'beloved,' 'approved in Christ,' 'labour in the Lord.'
days.context: Several of these names were common among slaves and freed slaves in Rome, which suggests the church drew people from many social levels.

word.why: Paul calls several people 'beloved' (vv. 8, 9, 12). After fifteen chapters of theology, he shows that the gospel creates real affection among people who might never otherwise have shared a table.

questions.q: Which people does Paul describe as labouring 'in the Lord' (v. 12)?
Why do you think Paul includes so many personal greetings in a letter so full of theology?
Who in your church family would you want to greet by name, and what would you say about them?

checkIn.q: How does Paul tell them to greet one another (v. 16)?
Whose mother does Paul call 'his mother and mine'?

days.title: To God Only Wise
days.focus: Paul warns against those who cause divisions, passes on greetings from his companions, and closes with a long doxology. Notice how the ending echoes the beginning: the gospel, the prophets, and 'the obedience of faith.'
days.context: Tertius, who wrote the letter down as Paul dictated it, adds his own greeting (v. 22). The promise that God will bruise Satan under their feet (v. 20) echoes Genesis 3:15.

word.why: Paul ends with 'the obedience of faith' among all nations (v. 26), the same phrase he used at the very start (1:5). The whole letter is framed by faith that responds to God in trusting obedience.

questions.q: What does Paul tell believers to do about those who cause divisions (v. 17)?
How does the closing doxology (vv. 25–27) sum up the message of Romans?
After eight weeks in Romans, what one truth do you most want to hold on to?

checkIn.q: Who wrote this letter down for Paul?
What will the God of peace bruise under their feet?

leader.intro: This study meets once a week for eight weeks, covering the five passages each member read that week. Plan 60–75 minutes: 10 minutes to settle in, 45 minutes of discussion, and 10–15 minutes of prayer. Romans is an argument that builds, so begin each session with a two-minute recap of where Paul has been and where he is going; a simple outline on a whiteboard or shared note helps. Some weeks raise questions on which faithful Christians disagree (especially chapters 7, 9, and 11); your job is not to settle them but to help the group read carefully and listen to one another.

sessions.title: Everyone Needs Rescue
sessions.opening: When have you received news that was genuinely good, the kind you couldn't wait to tell someone?
discussion: Read 1:16-17 aloud. In your own words, what is Paul's thesis for the whole letter?
In 1:18-32, what does Paul say went wrong with humanity, and what is the pattern of 'exchange'?
How does 2:1 turn the tables on the reader? Why do you think Paul builds his argument this way?
What advantages did the Jewish people have (2:17-20; 3:1-2), and why weren't they enough?
Paul concludes that 'all the world' is guilty before God (3:19). How does that land with you?
Why might Paul spend nearly three chapters on bad news before he gets to the solution?
sessions.notes: Paul wrote Romans around AD 57 to house churches he had never visited, made up of Jewish and Gentile believers. Emperor Claudius had expelled Jews from Rome around AD 49 (see Acts 18:2), and when they returned, Gentile believers may have become the majority, which helps explain why Paul addresses both groups so carefully. The first section (1:18–3:20) is one long argument that everyone, Gentile and Jew, needs God's righteousness; groups often treat 1:18-32 in isolation, but Paul's real target arrives in 2:1 with the person who judges others. Paul's list in 1:24-32 includes sexual sins and many others such as envy, gossip, and pride; if conversation fixes on one item, gently point back to Paul's point that the whole list describes all of us. Expect some to feel this section is heavy. It is meant to be: the bad news makes the good news of 3:21 shine. If someone asks about people who never hear the gospel, note that 1:20 and 2:14-15 speak to what people know, but Paul is not trying to answer every question here.
sessions.prayer: Thank God for the gospel, and confess together that all of us need his rescue.

sessions.title: Justified by Faith
sessions.opening: Have you ever received a gift you knew you could never repay? How did it feel?
discussion: What changes with the words 'But now' in 3:21? List the key words Paul uses in 3:21-26.
Why is boasting excluded (3:27)? What would boasting look like today?
Why does Paul choose Abraham as his example in chapter 4? What about Abraham's faith stands out?
In 5:1-11, what does Paul say we have now that we are justified?
Read 5:8. How does the timing of Christ's death show God's love?
What is the 'much more' in 5:12-21, and why does Paul keep emphasizing it?
sessions.notes: Romans 3:21-26 is often called the heart of the letter. Key words: 'justified' is a law-court word meaning declared in the right; 'redemption' comes from buying a slave's freedom; 'propitiation' (hilasterion) is the word used for the mercy seat on the ark of the covenant, where atonement was made. Christians have explained exactly how Christ's death deals with sin in several complementary ways, and it is fine to let the group notice the different pictures Paul uses. Chapter 4 can raise a question: does James 2 contradict Paul? Most readers see Paul addressing how one becomes right with God and James addressing the kind of faith that proves real, but don't let the session be swallowed by it. In chapter 5, the Adam-and-Christ comparison raises questions about original sin; Christian traditions explain it differently, so focus on Paul's main point that grace is stronger than sin. Encourage people to notice how personal 5:1-11 is: peace, access, hope, love poured into hearts.
sessions.prayer: Thank God for peace with him through Jesus Christ, and pray for anyone in the group who struggles to believe they are truly forgiven.

sessions.title: Freedom from Sin
sessions.opening: What is a habit you once had that you are glad to be free of, or one you wish you could break?
discussion: Paul anticipates the objection 'Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound?' Why would someone ask that after chapter 5?
How does baptism picture dying and rising with Christ (6:3-11)?
What does it mean to 'reckon' yourself dead to sin and alive to God?
Paul says everyone is a slave to something (6:16). What does that mean in everyday life?
How does the marriage illustration in 7:1-6 help explain the believer's relationship to the law?
Read 7:15-25. Does this struggle feel familiar? What hope does verse 25 offer?
sessions.notes: Chapter 6 answers the charge that grace makes sin unimportant; Paul's answer is that believers have been united with Christ in his death and resurrection, so sin no longer has the last word over them. Christians practice and understand baptism differently (infants or believers, sprinkling or immersion), but all agree that this passage speaks of union with Christ; keep the conversation there rather than on debates about method. Chapter 7 is one of the most debated passages in Romans: some read 7:14-25 as Paul's experience as a mature believer still battling sin; others as a description of life under the law without the Spirit, or of Israel's experience. Each reading is held by thoughtful Christians. Either way, the passage shows that the law is good but powerless to free us, and it sets up chapter 8. Many group members will relate personally to 7:15-19; let them, and point them to the thanksgiving of 7:25 and to next week's reading.
sessions.prayer: Pray for freedom in specific areas where members feel stuck, and thank God for deliverance through Jesus Christ.

sessions.title: Life in the Spirit
sessions.opening: What is a promise someone made to you that you have always been able to count on?
discussion: Read 8:1 aloud. Why does 'no condemnation' matter so much after chapter 7?
What does the Spirit do in this chapter? Make a list as a group.
What does it mean to be adopted as God's child (8:14-17)? How might that change the way someone prays?
Paul says creation, believers, and the Spirit all groan (8:18-27). What are they groaning for?
How do you understand 8:28? What does verse 29 add?
Which line of 8:31-39 do you most need to believe this week?
sessions.notes: Many readers consider Romans 8 the high point of the letter. The Holy Spirit, mentioned only a handful of times in chapters 1–7, now appears again and again. 'Flesh' in Paul usually means human nature apart from God, not the body itself, so watch for anyone thinking Paul is against physical life. 8:28 is often quoted to mean everything will turn out the way we hope; in context, the 'good' is being conformed to Christ (v. 29), and Paul is writing to people facing suffering (vv. 18, 35-36). The words 'foreknow' and 'predestinate' (vv. 29–30) have been understood differently, some emphasizing God's sovereign choice and others his foreknowledge of human faith; acknowledge this briefly and keep the focus on the assurance Paul intends. Verse 26 is a great comfort to people who feel they don't know how to pray. Consider closing by reading 8:31-39 aloud together.
sessions.prayer: Pray 'Abba, Father' together, bringing the group's groanings to God and thanking him that nothing can separate us from his love.

sessions.title: God's Faithfulness and Israel
sessions.opening: Who is someone you care about deeply who does not share your faith?
discussion: How does Paul feel about his fellow Israelites (9:1-5; 10:1)? Why does he start here?
What question is Paul answering in chapter 9? Why does it matter whether God's word has 'taken none effect' (9:6)?
What do the examples of Isaac and Jacob show about how God's promise moves forward?
How does Paul respond to the objection that God is unfair (9:14-24)?
Why did Israel stumble, according to 9:30–10:4?
In 10:9-17, what does Paul say is needed for someone to call on the Lord? What part do ordinary believers play?
sessions.notes: Chapters 9–11 are not a detour; they answer a question raised by everything before: if God's promises were made to Israel, and many Israelites have not believed in the Messiah, has God's word failed? Romans 9 has been read in very different ways. Some Christians (often called Reformed or Calvinist) see God's sovereign choice of individuals for salvation; others (often called Arminian or Wesleyan, as well as many Catholic and Orthodox readers) see God's choice of people and nations for roles in his plan, or the election of a people rather than individuals. Both sides take the text seriously and both have produced faithful believers. Your goal is not to resolve this debate but to help the group see what Paul says: God is faithful, mercy is never earned, and Paul's response to all of this is grief and prayer for his people (9:2-3; 10:1). Some may be troubled by 9:13 ('Esau have I hated'); it may help to note that it quotes Malachi 1:2-3 and that many interpreters understand 'loved' and 'hated' here as a Hebrew way of saying 'chosen' and 'not chosen' or 'loved less' (compare Luke 14:26). End with chapter 10's wide invitation: 'whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.'
sessions.prayer: Pray by name for people you love who do not yet believe, and for those who are sent to preach the good news.

sessions.title: Mercy for All, Lives Offered
sessions.opening: Have you ever been welcomed into a family or group you did not grow up in? What made you feel at home?
discussion: How does Paul show that God has not cast away his people (11:1-10)?
What does the olive tree picture (11:17-24) teach Gentile believers about humility?
What do you make of Paul's ending of chapter 11 in praise (11:33-36) rather than a neat conclusion?
Romans 12 begins with 'therefore.' How does God's mercy (chapters 1–11) lead to the call to be a living sacrifice?
What does it look like to be 'transformed by the renewing of your mind' in daily life?
Which command in 12:9-21 is most needed in our group or church right now?
sessions.notes: Romans 11 completes Paul's argument about Israel. Paul warns Gentile believers not to look down on Jewish people, a warning that sadly has often been ignored in church history; it is worth naming that history honestly. The phrase 'all Israel shall be saved' (11:26) is understood in several ways: a future large-scale turning of the Jewish people to Christ, the full number of God's people from Jews and Gentiles, or the elect remnant across history. Christians hold each view; avoid making any one a test of faithfulness. Paul's doxology in 11:33-36 is the right response to questions we can't fully answer. Chapter 12 is the turning point from belief to practice; 'reasonable service' can also mean 'spiritual worship,' and 'living sacrifice' contrasts with animals killed on altars. In 12:9-21, the commands come quickly; have the group pick a few rather than trying to cover all of them. 'Coals of fire' (12:20) quotes Proverbs 25:21-22 and is usually read as kindness that brings an enemy to remorse, not as a clever form of revenge.
sessions.prayer: Offer yourselves to God as living sacrifices, and pray for genuine love in your group and church.

sessions.title: Love in Community
sessions.opening: What is a minor preference (food, music, tradition) that people in your church care about more than you expected?
discussion: What reasons does Paul give for respecting governing authorities (13:1-7)? What limits might there be?
Paul says love is the fulfilling of the law (13:8-10). How does love 'fulfill' commands like 'Thou shalt not steal'?
What does 'put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ' (13:14) look like in practice?
What were the 'weak' and 'strong' disagreeing about in chapter 14? What might be similar disagreements today?
How does Paul ask both sides to behave toward each other?
How does Christ's example in 15:1-7 shape how we welcome one another?
sessions.notes: Romans 13:1-7 has been used in history to justify unjust rulers, which was not Paul's purpose. Paul wrote early in Nero's reign, and he describes government's God-given role in restraining evil. Christians have long taught that obedience to rulers has limits when they command what God forbids (Acts 5:29), and they differ on how to apply this; help the group discuss it without turning the session into a political debate. In chapter 14, the 'weak' are probably believers (many of them Jewish) who kept food laws and holy days, and the 'strong' felt free of these; Paul counts himself among the strong (15:1) but asks them to give way in love. Distinguish carefully between 'disputable matters' (chapter 14) and core beliefs or clear moral commands; Paul isn't saying nothing matters. 15:1-13 brings the whole letter's concern for Jew and Gentile together: Christ welcomed both, so they should welcome each other and praise God with one voice.
sessions.prayer: Pray for unity and patience among believers who disagree, and for wisdom and justice for those in authority.

sessions.title: Mission and Friendship
sessions.opening: Who is someone who helped you grow in faith, whose name most people would not know?
discussion: How does Paul describe his ministry in 15:14-21? What stands out about his ambition?
What were Paul's travel plans, and what do we know about how they actually turned out (see Acts 21–28)?
Why do you think the collection for Jerusalem mattered so much to Paul?
Read through the names in 16:1-16. What do you notice about the people Paul greets?
How does the closing doxology (16:25-27) connect back to how the letter began (1:1-5)?
Looking back over eight weeks, what has changed in how you understand the gospel?
sessions.notes: The end of Romans is easy to skim, but it shows the gospel at work in real relationships. Paul's plan was to bring the collection to Jerusalem and then go to Rome and on to Spain; Acts tells us he was arrested in Jerusalem and came to Rome as a prisoner (Acts 21–28), and whether he ever reached Spain is uncertain. Romans 16 names many women and men; Phoebe (likely the letter's carrier) is called a diakonos, which can mean servant or deacon, and verse 7 mentions Andronicus and Junia, 'of note among the apostles.' Christians differ on what these descriptions imply for church roles, and it is fine to say so without resolving it. Many of the names were common among slaves and freed slaves, showing a church that crossed social lines. The final doxology echoes 1:1-5 ('obedience of faith'), bookending the letter. Use some of the session to reflect on the whole study: what Paul has taught about sin, grace, the Spirit, God's faithfulness, and love in community.
sessions.prayer: Thank God by name for the people who have shaped your faith, and give glory 'to God only wise' through Jesus Christ.
